key_insight: Among Nigerian children under five with recent fever, the biggest gaps are getting tested after seeking care and receiving ACT among those treated, with caregiver financial barriers strongly linked to poorer ACT receipt.
clinical_relevance: This study suggests malaria programs may need to address both access and treatment-quality barriers, especially costs that prevent timely, guideline-concordant care.
method: Analyzed 3,962 febrile children under 5 from the 2023–24 Nigeria DHS.
Defined two cascade outcomes: Gap A (care-seeking plus diagnostic blood testing) and Gap B (ACT-only among children who received any antimalarial).
Compared survey-weighted logistic regression, elastic-net, random forest, and XGBoost using a held-out test set.
evidence_signal: Model discrimination was weak overall, with AUCs from 0.48 to 0.62 across eight models and 95% CIs spanning 0.50 for every model.
watch_item: Because predictive performance was near chance, the findings are more useful for identifying broad system barriers than for individual-level prediction or deployment.
paper_title: Antimalarial Pharmacotherapy Gaps in Nigerian Children Under Five: A Predictive Machine Learning Analysis of Care-Seeking, Testing, and ACT Treatment Using NDHS 2023-24
